frameworks.name: BANT Qualification
frameworks.definition: A four-criteria lead qualification filter — Budget, Authority, Need, Timing — used to determine whether a prospect should receive time or a lead magnet before a sales conversation.

frameworks.name: Lead Magnet Quality Framework
frameworks.definition: Four attributes that make a lead magnet effective: fast, easy, narrow, solves one complete problem — the solution reveals the next problem that the paid offer solves.

frameworks.name: Three Ps of Acquisition Process
frameworks.definition: Product, Prospect, Process — the three variables that determine VSL length and sales approach design before building any conversion asset.

frameworks.name: More, Better, New Scaling Sequence
frameworks.definition: Before opening a new acquisition channel, do more of what already works, then make it better; only pursue new channels after existing ones are maximized.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that blending cold-traffic conversion metrics with warm or high-intent conversion metrics is one of the biggest measurement mistakes business owners make, because the two audiences require different processes and sometimes different products — comparing them produces false conclusions about business health.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business using both paid cold traffic and warm/referral/search traffic simultaneously
claims.mechanism: Cold and warm audiences have different decision-making states and therefore different conversion rates; treating them as one population produces an average that is meaningless for either segment.
bounded_by: Businesses with only one traffic source do not face this blending problem

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a well-designed lead magnet — one that solves a narrow, complete problem and reveals the next problem the paid offer solves — can increase the number of buyers from 1% to roughly 3% of total traffic, tripling sales without increasing ad spend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Offer sold through inbound funnel with opt-in step
Lead magnet is high-quality and congruent with the core offer
claims.mechanism: Giving a free narrow solution before the money ask raises participation rate from ~1 in 100 to ~1 in 10, and converts ~3 of those 10 into buyers — net 3x improvement over direct ask.

numbers.axis: Conversion rate from traffic to paid customer

bounded_by: Lead magnet must solve a narrow complete problem and reveal the next problem, not just solve the core problem

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the quality of a lead magnet is load-bearing for long-term business reputation: the marketplace judges a business by its worst free content, so a low-quality lead magnet ensures that 99% of prospects will never convert to paid customers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses competing for trust in a market where comparison is easy
claims.mechanism: The lead magnet is the first material contact with the brand; poor quality sets a floor expectation that suppresses willingness to pay for the premium offer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that applying BANT qualification (Budget, Authority, Need, Timing) before delivering a personalized lead magnet prevents wasted delivery effort and also signals exclusivity — which converts hesitant maybes into yeses because prospects infer the service only accepts serious, qualified buyers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: High-touch service business where lead magnet delivery has real cost
Business can credibly exclude unqualified prospects
claims.mechanism: Qualification signals market positioning to the prospect ('they only serve people like me'), converting borderline buyers through social proof of exclusivity rather than losing them via friction.
bounded_by: Does not apply to self-serve or low-cost lead magnet contexts where delivery cost is near zero

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a Video Sales Letter (VSL) placed before a sales call reduces the number of calls required to close a prospect and can compress individual call length from 60-90 minutes to 15-20 minutes, because it front-loads all the information a prospect needs to make a decision.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business currently requiring 2+ calls or 60+ minute calls to close
VSL is short enough (3-7 minutes for high-intent traffic) that prospects will watch it before the call
claims.mechanism: A decision only requires the information needed to make it; front-loading that information via video eliminates call-by-call information transfer, so the sales conversation starts at decision-readiness rather than education.

anchors.value: 15-20 minute calls, potentially 1 call to close

bounded_by: VSL length must match traffic intent: high-intent traffic needs only 3-7 minutes; cold traffic may require longer

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that if a sales process currently requires 2 calls to close, reducing it to 1 call by adding pre-selling components doubles sales output with the same sales team size.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Headcount of sales team is held constant
Call quality and lead quality remain equivalent
claims.mechanism: Sales team capacity is measured in number of calls; halving calls required per close doubles the number of closes achievable in the same time period.

numbers.axis: Sales closes per unit of team capacity

bounded_by: Assumes lead quality is maintained — reducing calls by rushing an unready prospect does not double sales

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a funnel headline should follow the structure 'how to achieve [desired outcome] without [biggest fear/objection],' because the headline frames every downstream piece of copy and determines 80% of the advertising dollar's effectiveness.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Landing page or funnel with a headline as the first visible element
claims.mechanism: The headline sets the interpretive frame for all subsequent copy; a frame that matches the prospect's emotional state (desire + fear) increases the probability all copy is read and processed favorably.

numbers.axis: Share of advertising dollar attributed to headline

anchors.region: Body copy and remaining page elements

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a fashion stylist business (Ashley's case), 6 affiliate partners sourced through 40 cold emails accounted for one third of total annual revenue ($103,000 of ~$309,000), making the per-email revenue value approximately $2,500 — metrics that would be considered extraordinary by any paid acquisition standard.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: High-touch service business (personal styling) targeting affluent clientele
Affiliates (matchmakers, social clubs) naturally serve the same target audience
claims.mechanism: Affiliates send pre-qualified warm prospects who have already demonstrated willingness to pay for premium services — these convert at significantly higher rates than cold traffic.

numbers.axis: Revenue per cold email sent to affiliate prospects

bounded_by: Requires natural audience overlap — affiliate's clients must already be the ideal customer for the service

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most founders fail to scale their best-performing acquisition channel because they are distracted by managing delivery, clients, pricing, and employees simultaneously, making it cognitively difficult to identify and double down on the channel generating the highest return.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Early-to-mid stage business where founder still handles multiple operational functions
claims.mechanism: Cognitive load from operational complexity prevents the founder from adopting a strategic perspective ('what one thing would double my business?') — the answer is usually in plain sight but invisible due to bandwidth constraints.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that affiliate partners must be treated like customers — actively nurtured, engaged, and retained through regular outreach, value delivery (e.g., events for their clients), and relationship investment — because affiliates who are not actively managed will stop sending referrals.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Affiliate channel used for ongoing lead generation (not one-time partnerships)
claims.mechanism: Affiliates have competing priorities; without consistent engagement and value delivery they de-prioritize your referral relationship — the pipeline dries up without maintenance.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a business targeting luxury or affluent buyers, a premium price anchor tier — even if only 10% of customers select it — both doubles total revenue contribution from that tier and makes the previously most-expensive tier feel like a deal to the remaining 90%.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business with an existing high-tier continuity offer
New anchor tier priced at ~10x the existing continuity price
Affluent or luxury buyer segment where higher price signals higher status
claims.mechanism: Cognitive anchoring makes the previously expensive tier appear affordable by comparison to the new highest tier; the 10x pricing on 10% of buyers produces revenue equivalent to adding the original tier's full revenue again.

numbers.axis: Revenue impact of adding anchor tier priced at 10x base

anchors.value: no revenue change; base tier perception unchanged
effectively doubles total revenue vs. base-only pricing

bounded_by: Veblen good dynamics apply to luxury segments; commodity or price-sensitive segments respond differently

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the point of maximum gross profit for a business is typically after the point of maximum conversion rate — meaning most businesses underprice their offers and could raise prices significantly before total revenue decreases.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service or product with inelastic demand from target segment
Price is currently set below market-clearing level (high close rate is a diagnostic signal)
claims.mechanism: Revenue is price multiplied by volume; if price increases by 3x and volume falls by half, total revenue increases by 1.5x. Maximum conversion does not equal maximum profit.

numbers.axis: Price vs. gross profit along a demand curve

anchors.region: Maximum conversion rate (lowest price that works)
anchors.value: high volume, lower gross profit per unit

anchors.region: Point of maximum gross profit (higher price, lower volume)
anchors.value: lower conversion, higher total gross profit

bounded_by: Does not apply where brand reputation depends on volume (e.g., market share battles)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for high-end luxury buyers, raising price can actually increase demand (Veblen good effect) because expensive pricing signals superiority — and if status-seeking buyers are not given a premium path, they default to the cheapest available tier instead.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Affluent buyer segment (CEOs, socialites, high-income earners) where status signaling is a purchase motivation
Product or service where higher price credibly signals higher quality or exclusivity
claims.mechanism: Status-seeking buyers interpret price as a quality signal; absence of a premium tier forces them into the cheapest available option because there is no signal of superiority to act on.
bounded_by: Does not apply to commodity markets, price-comparison shopping, or audiences without status motivations

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that re-positioning the continuity upsell as the default next step after onboarding — rather than a separate repitch — increases take rates by leveraging human default bias: people assume what most others do is lower-risk and follow the default path.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with an onboarding phase followed by an optional continuity offering
Upsell framed as the natural continuation of onboarding, not a new sales conversation
claims.mechanism: Humans use default choices as a heuristic for safety ('if most people do this, it has already been tested and is lower risk'); opt-out framing exploits this bias to shift baseline behavior from opt-in (low) to opt-out (high). Classic reference: organ donor opt-out countries achieve 70%+ participation vs. <10% for opt-in countries.

numbers.axis: Participation rate by opt-in vs. opt-out framing

bounded_by: Default bias works when the default is perceived as credible and safe — a poorly delivered onboarding negates it

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a premium business must maintain sales process congruence across every touchpoint — ads, lead magnet, qualification, pricing, and product delivery — because any single break in congruence signals a frame break that drops conversion rates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: High-end or boutique service business with premium pricing
claims.mechanism: Buyers calibrate trust by pattern-matching every touchpoint against the premium promise; a mismatch (e.g., luxury brand with a generic intake form) triggers cognitive dissonance that registers as 'something feels off' and suppresses willingness to pay.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that staying focused on a single specific avatar enables partnership with adjacent non-competitive businesses that serve the same avatar — making focus a prerequisite for affiliate channel strategy, not just for offer design.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business where affiliate/referral partnerships are a desired channel
claims.mechanism: Adjacent businesses (e.g., divorce attorneys, executive coaches) can only refer with confidence if they know exactly who you serve; a diffuse avatar makes referral uncertain and eliminates the partner's motivation to send clients.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a VSL built iteratively — starting with a first version and adding objection-handling segments over time based on live sales call recordings — is more effective than trying to build a perfect VSL upfront, because the best objections surface only after real prospect interactions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business with an active sales process and call recordings
claims.mechanism: Objection patterns reveal prospect information gaps; adding pre-recorded answers to the VSL eliminates those gaps before the live call, which compresses call length and increases close rate.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a high-intent traffic source (e.g., referrals, search), a VSL of 3-7 minutes is sufficient to pre-sell and set expectations before a sales call, because high-intent prospects arrive with most information already present and need only confirmation, not education.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Traffic source is high-intent (search, referral, direct inquiry)
Sales call follows the VSL

numbers.axis: VSL length by traffic intent level

bounded_by: Low-intent or cold traffic requires longer VSL to build context before the call

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that sending 40 cold emails to build an affiliate network — a one-time effort most founders never attempt — can generate one third of total business revenue, making affiliate outreach the highest-return acquisition activity for most service businesses relative to effort invested.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business where a natural adjacent audience exists in non-competing businesses
Founder or designated relationship manager can sustain affiliate activation

numbers.axis: Revenue generated per unit of outreach effort

anchors.region: 40 emails to matchmakers and social clubs (Ashley's case)
anchors.value: 6 partners = ~$103k = 1/3 of total revenue = $2,500 per email
rare to achieve $2,500 revenue per ad dollar or per email equivalent

bounded_by: Requires adjacent non-competing businesses that organically encounter the ideal customer

examples.text: Ashley (a fashion stylist) was generating $309,000 in annual revenue with 42% margins ($130k profit), selling an $8,500 60-day onboarding package followed by $2,000/month or $4,500/quarter ongoing styling. Despite a strong close rate and loyal customers, her funnel had no headline, no value proposition, and no lead magnet — just a 'get more info' button. She was receiving 1,800 clicks but converting only 8 to sales (0.4% conversion rate), revealing a massive leak in the funnel rather than a product or pricing problem. Alex Hormozi used her business as a live case study to demonstrate the three core lever categories: funnel conversion, affiliate activation, and pricing.

Alex Hormozi described a lead magnet he encountered in the dating niche: 'How to know if a girl wants you to kiss her on a date.' The magnet solved a single, narrow, high-pain problem with a specific behavioral test (brushing her hair behind her ear) and delivered immediate perceived value. It demonstrated the ideal lead magnet structure: fast, easy, narrow, solves one complete problem, and reveals the next problem (escalating the relationship) that the paid offer addresses.

Alex Hormozi cited the organ donor opt-out country example: one country achieved 70%+ citizen participation in organ donation by making donation the default and requiring citizens to actively opt out, while every other country using opt-in framing remained below 10%. He applied this directly to Ashley's continuity upsell — by making continuity the assumed next step after onboarding ('let's make sure your transformation sticks') rather than a fresh repitch, take rates increase through default bias without changing the offer.

Ashley sourced 6 high-leverage affiliate partners (matchmakers, social clubs) through 40 cold emails she sent over her business lifetime — yet those 6 partners delivered one third of her entire revenue. When Hormozi asked how many emails it took to land them, she said 40. He then challenged her: if 40 emails produced a third of her business (roughly $103k), would she not send 400? He committed her to 20 outreach emails per day to scale from 6 to potentially 60 partners, projecting a proportional revenue increase from the affiliate channel alone.

Ashley expanded her affiliate avatar from matchmakers only to include private social clubs, executive coaches, high-end personal trainers, and divorce attorneys — all businesses that serve affluent single executives or status-conscious couples without competing with her styling service. A divorce attorney loses nothing by referring a divorce client to a fashion stylist; the referral actually adds value to the attorney's client relationship. This example illustrates how avatar focus (single customer type) enables partnership with all non-competing businesses serving that avatar.

Ashley had recently changed her prices to $2,000/month or $4,500/quarter for continuity, but most of her existing clients were grandfathered at $1,500/quarter or less. The website and intake process revealed no pricing information until after the call — no tiers, no value framing, no premium signals — effectively delivering a luxury service through a commodity sales process. Hormozi identified congruence failure: premium brand positioning requires premium signals at every touchpoint from the first ad to the intake form.

practices.text: Build the affiliate list by starting with your current avatar and asking: what other businesses serve this same customer at this same life moment? Do not limit to obvious partners; adjacent businesses (personal trainers, coaches, attorneys) may have equal or better audiences.
Rewrite funnel headlines to focus on the free offer (lead magnet) rather than the paid product; the headline should lower the commitment barrier to a first step, not close the sale.

When a prospect shows up to a sales call without having watched the VSL, maintain the call frame by pausing the call, playing the short VSL in the session ('grab a coffee, back in seven minutes'), and resuming — rather than running alternate scripts for watched vs. unwatched prospects.
Fix funnel leaks before scaling ad spend; confirming the funnel converts at an acceptable rate before increasing traffic prevents compounding waste.

When designing a price anchor tier, make it as similar as possible to the core offer but with one or two premium differentiators most buyers will not need — this maximizes cognitive anchor effect while keeping the feature gap believable.

Track and separate conversion metrics for cold traffic vs. warm/high-intent traffic; blend only when you want to assess overall business health, never to evaluate funnel performance or channel effectiveness.

When building a VSL, record a first version and get it live; then listen to sales call objections, record additional objection-answer segments, and append them to the existing VSL with a 'got some more questions, answering them now' framing.
